identity.title: Capillary refill time prolonged (>2-3 s, fingertip at heart level, warm room)

technique.how: With the hand at heart level in a warm room, press the distal phalanx of the index finger with firm pressure for 10-15 s (until blanched), release, and time return of the original color with a stopwatch. Normal <=2-3 s in adults; also assessable at the knee. Standardize pressure and lighting and repeat once.
technique.prerequisites: Warm extremity and ambient temperature; remove nail polish; use a stopwatch or count aloud rather than estimating.
technique.contraindications: None; unreliable in peripheral vascular disease, Raynaud phenomenon, cold environment, or vasopressor-induced peripheral vasoconstriction.

interpretation.positive_finding: Prolonged CRT (index >2.4-3 s) after initial resuscitation of septic shock marks persistent hypoperfusion and roughly doubles the probability of early death; it is a target for resuscitation rather than a diagnostic sign of a specific shock type.
interpretation.negative_finding: A normal CRT is reassuring for tissue perfusion but does not exclude mild-to-moderate hypovolemia (sensitivity 6-46% in adults) or shock; do not use it to rule out volume depletion.
interpretation.pitfalls: Cold, age, sex, ambient light, pressure applied and observer timing all change CRT; the 1999 RCE concluded CRT has no proven diagnostic value for hypovolemia in adults, and poorly measured CRT loses prognostic accuracy.
interpretation.changes_what: Persistently prolonged CRT in shock should prompt reassessment of perfusion (lactate, fluids/vasoactives) and escalation; normal CRT should not lower suspicion of hypovolemia.

estimates.population: 13 adult ED patients with history suggestive of hypovolemia and hypotension, vs 47 euvolemic blood-donor controls; CRT scored against age-sex-specific upper limits of normal
estimates.reference_standard: Clinical classification (hypotension with suggestive history) before rehydration
estimates.quote: sensitivity ... was 6% for the 450-mL blood loss group, 26% for the orthostatic group, and 46% for the hypotensive group

estimates.target_condition: Hypovolemia (clinical history plus abnormal orthostatic vital signs)
estimates.population: 19 adult ED patients with history suggestive of hypovolemia and abnormal orthostatic vital signs, vs 47 euvolemic blood-donor controls
estimates.reference_standard: Clinical classification (abnormal orthostatic vital signs with suggestive history) before rehydration
estimates.quote: sensitivity ... was 6% for the 450-mL blood loss group, 26% for the orthostatic group, and 46% for the hypotensive group

estimates.target_condition: 14-day mortality (prognostic) after 6 h of septic shock resuscitation; index-finger CRT >2.4 s
estimates.population: 59 consecutive adult septic shock patients in a tertiary ICU, measured at H6
estimates.computed_from: LR+ = 0.82/(1-0.73) = 3.04; LR- = (1-0.82)/0.73 = 0.25; from abstract sensitivity 82% and specificity 73%
estimates.quote: index CRT at 2.4 s predicted 14-day outcome with a sensitivity of 82% (95% CI [60-95]) and a specificity of 73% (95% CI [56-86])

estimates.target_condition: Death (prognostic) in adults with acute circulatory failure; abnormal CRT at study-specific threshold
estimates.population: 13 studies of adults with established acute circulatory failure (septic and other shock), ED and ICU
estimates.computed_from: LR+ = 0.54/(1-0.72) = 1.93; LR- = (1-0.54)/0.72 = 0.64; from pooled sensitivity 54% and specificity 72% (pooled DOR 3.4 [1.4-8.3])
estimates.quote: The pooled sensitivity was 54% (95%CI [43; 64]), and the pooled specificity was 72% (95%CI [55; 84])
estimates.location: Results, Primary analysis paragraph and Table 2 (PMC10693708 full text)

sources.citation: McGee S, Abernethy WB 3rd, Simel DL. The rational clinical examination. Is this patient hypovolemic? JAMA. 1999;281(11):1022-1029.
Schriger DL, Baraff LJ. Capillary refill--is it a useful predictor of hypovolemic states? Ann Emerg Med. 1991;20(6):601-605.
Ait-Oufella H, Bige N, Boelle PY, et al. Capillary refill time exploration during septic shock. Intensive Care Med. 2014;40(7):958-964.
Jacquet-Lagreze M, Wiart C, Schweizer R, et al. Prognostic value of capillary refill time in adult patients: a systematic review with meta-analysis. Crit Care. 2023;27(1):473.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use CRT to rule out hypovolemia or hemorrhage, and do not interpret it in a cold, vasopressor-constricted, or peripherally ischemic limb.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: CRT >3-4 s with hypotension, altered mentation, or mottling indicates shock with hypoperfusion; start resuscitation and escalate rather than repeating the sign.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Inter-rater concordance 80% (index) and 95% (knee) in Ait-Oufella 2014 with a standardized protocol; unstandardized estimation is poorly reproducible and the 2023 meta-analysis found accuracy higher only with high-quality measurement.

extraction_notes: Sens/spec entered as percent. Two evidence streams are kept separate: (1) diagnostic accuracy for hypovolemia in adults, which is poor — Schriger 1991 reports sensitivity only (specificity not given in the abstract; full text not in PMC), and the 1999 RCE abstract states CRT has 'no proven diagnostic value' in adults without giving numbers; the 6% sensitivity for 450-mL blood donors is in the same quote but was not entered as a separate row. (2) Prognostic accuracy for death in shock (Ait-Oufella 2014 single-center ICU; Jacquet-Lagreze 2023 pooled, high heterogeneity, thresholds varied across studies). These are prognostic, not diagnostic, estimates and the target_condition fields say so. LRs were computed from reported sens/spec. The seeded differentials (anaphylaxis, cardiogenic shock, septic shock) are not discriminated from each other by CRT; it grades perfusion, not etiology.
